items.title: Maps from the spectrum of a complete local Noetherian algebra agree with maps from its formal spectrum
items.author: The Stacks Project Authors

items.difficulty_reason: For a complete local Noetherian algebra R over a scheme S and an algebraic space X over S, the lemma asserts that the natural map from morphisms of the spectrum of R into X to morphisms of the formal spectrum of R into X is bijective (statement lines 7226-7236). The proof rewrites the target as the inverse limit of the morphism sets over the quotients of R by powers of the maximal ideal and then proves the two halves by different mechanisms. Injectivity measures the difference of two morphisms by the fibre product with the diagonal: what results is a scheme, locally of finite type, separated and locally quasi-finite over the spectrum of R, hence locally Noetherian, and the point over the closed point has a local ring whose quotients by the powers of the maximal ideal agree with those of R; since the local ring embeds in its completion, the local ring is R and the two morphisms agree (proof lines 7240-7262). Surjectivity is a lifting argument: a surjective etale cover of the space is chosen, the fibre of that cover over the residue field is a disjoint union of spectra of finite separable extensions so that a suitable finite separable extension and a compatible point are available, the corresponding finite etale extension of complete local rings is formed, formal etaleness of the cover lifts the given compatible family to the extension, the scheme case of the statement produces a morphism from the extended spectrum, and descent along the resulting fppf covering produces a morphism from the spectrum of R (proof lines 7264-7309). The claim is H3: injectivity rests on a completion argument through a fibre product with the diagonal, surjectivity on an etale lifting combined with fppf descent, and the compatibility needed to make the descent work is obtained by invoking the injectivity half again for the tensor square of the extension -- three separate ingredients rather than one.
